connection: Production repositories and models exist. ScratchPad retains earlier language experiments; no verified requirement needs a custom generic type or method. Preserve a generic-method experiment in ScratchPad because the production domain has no natural generic algorithm yet.
objectives: Identify at least three generic types already in real, everyday use across this codebase, and state what concrete type argument each is instantiated with.
Explain what ClockEntry communicates in IEnumerable<ClockEntry>: every value produced by the sequence has that element type.
Read Session14GenericMethodDemo.SelectGreater<T>(T left, T right) one piece at a time and explain what each use of T means.
Call SelectGreater<T> with both DateTime (ClockIn timestamps) and int (EmployeeId values) and confirm one method definition serves both.

visuals.title: Generic types are filled in at each use site
visuals.explanation: List<ClockEntry>, Dictionary<int, Employee>, and IEnumerable<ClockEntry> are generic type definitions whose placeholders have been filled with the concrete types this application needs.

visuals.title: A generic method infers T from its arguments
visuals.explanation: SelectGreater(entryA.ClockIn, entryB.ClockIn) infers T as DateTime from the arguments' actual type -- no explicit SelectGreater<DateTime> is required.

visuals.title: IEnumerable<ClockEntry> identifies its element type
visuals.explanation: Session 13 established that IEnumerable<T> promises enumeration. Supplying ClockEntry for T tells the compiler and caller that each value produced during enumeration is a ClockEntry.

visuals.title: One method definition, many closed types
visuals.explanation: SelectGreater<DateTime> and SelectGreater<int> are two different closed generic methods generated from the one open SelectGreater<T> definition, at compile time.

preQuiz.prompt: What are List<T>, Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, and IEnumerable<T> called before concrete types are supplied?
options: Open generic types -- they define a shape with placeholder type parameters that must be filled in (with ClockEntry, or int and Employee) at the point of use
preQuiz.explanation: A generic type definition like List<T> is not usable on its own -- List<ClockEntry> is the closed, concrete type actually declared and used.

preQuiz.prompt: What does ClockEntry communicate in the type IEnumerable<ClockEntry>?
options: ClockEntry fills the T placeholder and tells the compiler that enumeration produces ClockEntry values
It means the sequence must contain exactly one ClockEntry
It gives IEnumerable an Add method for ClockEntry values
preQuiz.explanation: The type argument preserves element type information: foreach can give the caller a ClockEntry directly, while Session 13's narrower IEnumerable contract still does not promise Add or indexing.

preQuiz.prompt: Can Session14GenericMethodDemo.SelectGreater<T> be called with both DateTime and int arguments, using the same method definition?
options: Yes -- as long as the argument type implements IComparable<T> (both DateTime and int do), the compiler generates a specific closed version of SelectGreater<T> for each type used
No -- a separate SelectGreater method must be written for each type
Only with int, since DateTime cannot be compared
preQuiz.explanation: This is the entire value of generics: one definition, reused across every type that satisfies its constraint -- Session 15 studies that constraint directly.

concept.title: Generic types already everywhere in this codebase
paragraphs: ClockEntryRepository._clockEntries is List<ClockEntry> -- List<T> with T filled in as ClockEntry. EmployeeDirectory's employees field is Dictionary<int, Employee> -- Dictionary<TKey,TValue> with two type arguments supplied. IClockEntryRepository.GetEmployeeClockEntries returns IEnumerable<ClockEntry> -- IEnumerable<T> with T filled in as ClockEntry.
None of these are new concepts introduced by this session -- they are the same collection types earlier sessions already used, now being recognized explicitly as generic types.
concept.code:
List<ClockEntry> _clockEntries;              // List<T> with T = ClockEntry
Dictionary<int, Employee> employees;         // Dictionary<TKey,TValue> with TKey=int, TValue=Employee
IEnumerable<ClockEntry> entries;             // IEnumerable<T> with T = ClockEntry

concept.title: Start with the problem: two methods would repeat one decision
paragraphs: The ScratchPad experiment needs the greater of two employee IDs and the later of two clock-in times. You could write SelectGreaterInt and SelectGreaterDateTime, but both methods would make the same decision: compare two values and return the one that comes later or ranks higher.

The only meaningful difference between those two methods is the value type. A generic method replaces that changing type name with a type parameter, allowing one definition to preserve the caller's actual type.

concept.title: Read SelectGreater<T> from left to right
paragraphs: The first T is the return type: SelectGreater gives back the same type it compares. <T> after the method name declares T as this method's type parameter. The two parameter types say left and right must both be that same T.

For one call, every T in the signature becomes int. For another call, every T becomes DateTime. T is not a special runtime value and it does not mean 'any mixture of types'; it is a compile-time placeholder consistently filled for one call.

concept.title: The constraint gives T one required capability
paragraphs: Without more information, the compiler must assume T could be any type, so it cannot assume that left has a CompareTo method. The where T : IComparable<T> constraint narrows the allowed types to values that know how to compare themselves with another value of the same type.
Both int and DateTime satisfy that contract. Session 15 focuses on constraints; for this session, read this line as: T may vary, but it must be comparable to another T.

concept.title: CompareTo returns an ordering signal, not a Boolean
paragraphs: left.CompareTo(right) returns a negative number when left comes before right, zero when they are equal, and a positive number when left comes after right. SelectGreater only needs to distinguish 'left is at least as late or high' from 'right is later or higher.'

That is why the condition uses >= 0. Equal values return left; a positive result returns left; a negative result returns right. The same three-way signal works for 14 versus 27 and for 8:00 AM versus 9:30 AM.

concept.title: The compiler infers T separately for each call
paragraphs: When SelectGreater receives two EmployeeId values, both arguments are int, so the compiler treats that call as SelectGreater<int> and the result remains int. When it receives two ClockIn values, both are DateTime, so that call behaves as SelectGreater<DateTime> and the result remains DateTime.

You normally omit <int> and <DateTime> at the call site because the argument types provide enough information. This is generic method type inference: one method definition, checked as two type-safe uses without converting values to object or casting the results back.

concept.title: This is a teaching method, not an automatic production utility
paragraphs: SelectGreater<T> is useful here because its small body exposes generic syntax, type inference, a constraint, and CompareTo. That educational value does not mean every production application should create this helper.

In production, first check whether .NET already provides the operation you need. Math.Max handles many numeric types, a direct comparison can select between two DateTime values, and Comparer<T>.Default can perform a general comparison. Create a custom method only when its name and behavior express a real application need more clearly than the available framework operation.

lab.objective: Build one ScratchPad method that selects between two values while preserving their type, then call that same method with employee IDs and clock-in times.
lab.startingCondition: Session 13 established the session-specific ScratchPad class and Run method pattern. Preserve Domain and App unchanged; create a Session 14 ScratchPad class and append one Run call to the existing ScratchPad entry point.

steps.text: Stub Run first so this class follows the session-specific ScratchPad pattern established in Session 13.

Below Run, stub a private static generic method named SelectGreater. Read the signature from left to right: it returns T, declares T in <T>, and requires both parameters to be that same T. The constraint tells the compiler that T supplies CompareTo; Session 15 examines constraints in depth.
Build before implementing either method. A successful build proves that the generic method signature and its constraint are valid independently of the method behavior.

review: The lab uses scratchpad because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can List<ClockEntry> and Dictionary<int, Employee> both exist in the same codebase using the same underlying generic collection library?
options: List<T> and Dictionary<TKey,TValue> are separate generic type definitions in .NET's base class library, each independently instantiated with whatever type arguments the codebase needs
They are the same generic type used two different ways
Dictionary is built from List internally in every case
postQuiz.explanation: List<T> and Dictionary<TKey,TValue> are distinct generic types -- the shared idea is only that both defer their element/key/value types to a type parameter, filled in at each declaration.

postQuiz.prompt: What would happen if Session14GenericMethodDemo.SelectGreater<T> had no constraint at all (just SelectGreater<T>(T left, T right))?
options: left.CompareTo(right) would fail to compile -- without a constraint, the compiler only knows T could be any type, including one with no CompareTo method at all
It would work exactly the same for every type
T would default to object automatically
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly what Session 15 studies next -- without the where T : IComparable<T> constraint, the compiler cannot assume CompareTo exists on an arbitrary T.

postQuiz.prompt: Does calling SelectGreater(entryA.ClockIn, entryB.ClockIn) require writing SelectGreater<DateTime>(...) explicitly?
options: No -- the compiler infers T as DateTime from the argument types automatically; explicit type arguments are only needed when inference is ambiguous or impossible
Yes -- generic methods always require an explicit type argument
No -- but only because DateTime is a built-in type
postQuiz.explanation: Type inference from arguments is standard for generic methods in C# -- explicit type arguments (SelectGreater<DateTime>(...)) are optional here and rarely needed.

reflections: Why does writing SelectGreater<T> once, instead of SelectGreaterDateTime and SelectGreaterInt separately, matter beyond saving a few lines of code?
What other places in this codebase might benefit from a generic helper like SelectGreater<T>, once you start looking for duplicated type-specific logic?
How does IEnumerable<ClockEntry> communicate more to a reader than a non-generic collection whose element type is unknown?
whatBreaks: Calling Session14GenericMethodDemo.SelectGreater with two Employee arguments (instead of their EmployeeId or another IComparable value) fails to compile, because Employee implements no comparison logic -- this is the constraint doing its job, not a limitation to work around. Removing the where T : IComparable<T> constraint would let SelectGreater<T> accept any T at its boundary, but left.CompareTo(right) inside the method body would then fail to compile, since the compiler could no longer assume CompareTo exists.
summary: Generic types are not a new concept this session invents -- List<ClockEntry>, Dictionary<int, Employee>, and IEnumerable<ClockEntry> were already doing real work in earlier sessions. Session14GenericMethodDemo.SelectGreater<T> demonstrates the other half of generics: T consistently replaces the return and parameter types, the constraint supplies comparison capability, CompareTo reports ordering, and the compiler infers int or DateTime separately at each call.
